quote.author: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890)

macro.title: What It Means — VWRA, Bonds, Gold & BTC

reads.label: VWRA (held)
reads.text: two-sided into Wednesday — a Warsh hold plus a signed Hormuz formula is relief; a hike or resumed strikes cracks the eggshells, and Thursday's earnings swing it more than the Fed.

reads.label: Global bonds (held)
reads.text: the enemy is a hike plus sticky inflation plus any oil re-spike, all pressing the front end; the currency hedge cushions the firm dollar.

reads.label: Gold (read only)
reads.text: near its record, bid by both the war premium and stagflation-lite — the cleanest hedge on the board.

reads.label: Bitcoin (read only)
reads.text: range-bound around $64.5k, trading as high-beta risk, not gold's twin. The two he holds stay VWRA and global bonds; the two he only reads stay gold and BTC.

stories.headline: The Guns Stay Quiet, and Oman Drafts the Formula
stories.dek: A single held night has hardened into a third day of mutual restraint, and in Tehran an Omani delegation is drafting who runs the Strait of Hormuz. The document exists; the signatures do not. Two regional sources say any deal still needs Trump's approval — which is another way of saying the verdict is not in.

stories.headline: The Biggest Open Model Ever, Unloadable by Design
stories.dek: Moonshot's Kimi K3 — 2.8 trillion parameters — publishes its weights on Hugging Face at eight o'clock this morning, our time. It is the largest open-weights release in history and, for all but a handful of data centres, the least usable. "Open," this week, becomes a thing you can read about but not run.

stories.kicker: The Macro Desk · The Week Ahead
stories.headline: Two Central Banks, and the Question Is Still "Hike?"
stories.dek: Singapore rules this morning, the Fed on Wednesday, and the barrel has come off the boil on the Oman talks. A hold is the base case in both rooms — but the live tail in Washington is a hike, not a cut, and that is what keeps the dollar firm and the tape on eggshells. Market explanation, not investment advice.

stories.headline: Two Verdicts Land Before Lunch
stories.dek: The central bank rules this morning on a quarter that grew 5.7% and an inflation rate still mild — and it does so with a US forced-labour tariff now costed by the manufacturers themselves. The consensus is a hold. The interesting sentence will be the one about what comes next.

stories.headline: Turf City Opens Its Book, and Half of It Sells
stories.dek: Dunearn House moved 211 of 380 units at launch — the three-bedders sold out, but 55% is well shy of this year's ~76% norm. Correcting our own held figure from No. 53: the reflexive prime-district bid has a ceiling, and this is the clearest reading of it yet.

stories.headline: The FX5 Gets Its Number
stories.dek: Sony's first Open Gate Cinema Line body moves from "price TBA" to a real peg: US$4,899, pre-orders open, shipping mid-August. The differentiators — internal RAW and a full-frame open gate in a compact body — are exactly the ones that only prove out on footage.

stories.headline: Plain English Is Now the Default
stories.dek: Home Assistant's current release makes intent-based triggers the standard way to write an automation — "when the living room gets dark," not a page of entity plumbing. For a household migrating off Lutron's app onto HA, that is precisely the layer worth finishing the move for.

stories.headline: Gold on an Everyday Case, and an Argument About the Price
stories.dek: Grand Seiko's SBGH376 "Sakura-Wakaba" is the brand's first non-limited 62GS in solid yellow gold — a soft-yen-era object with a hard-currency sticker of S$41,400. It is exactly the tension this desk tracks: superb metal and finishing, against a resale market that still discounts the name.

stories.headline: The Verdict Breaks This Week — Without an IMAX Screen
stories.dek: Reactions to Spider-Man: Brand New Day post tonight, the review embargo lifts tomorrow, and Singapore sees it Thursday. The tracking says biggest opening of the year. The oddity says it is doing it on standard screens, because Nolan is holding the large-format ones.

stories.headline: The Timeline No Parent Set
stories.dek: Two new cohorts point the same way: the driver of a preteen's low mood may be the pace and timing of puberty itself, not her screen. Earlier-maturing children — girls and boys — carry higher odds of depression, and a hormone can move before anything shows. General guidance, not medical advice.

stories.headline: The Bumblebee Drinks the Dirtier Cup
stories.dek: Foraging the same fields as honeybees, bumblebees come home carrying several times as much toxic metal — arsenic, cadmium, lead — even in gentle English countryside. Same landscape, same flowers, very different dose. The dinner-party version: not all pollinators sip from the same glass.

stories.headline: Loneliness Looks Less Like a Symptom Than a Cause
stories.dek: A large new study runs three independent methods — observational, sibling-comparison and genetic — and they converge: loneliness may not merely travel with poor mental health, it may help drive it. It advances a story this desk has been tracking from "condition" to "cause."

stories.headline: The Cheapest Lever Is Eighty Minutes of Sleep
stories.dek: A randomised trial trimmed sleep by about eighty minutes a night for six weeks, and metabolically at-risk adults gained weight — with the mechanism being movement, not appetite. They didn't eat more; they moved less. For a busy forty-five-year-old, recovery is a training variable, not a luxury. Not medical advice.

stories.headline: The Autumn Calendar Hardens
stories.dek: Race week grows its bill again, a K-pop anniversary tour lands, and the spring racing carnival down under comes into booking range — the dated agenda for a reader planning September to November.

stories.headline: The Sealed Room
stories.dek: This week a reader waits on half a dozen verdicts — two central banks, a Gulf transit deal, a film's embargo, a model's release. It is worth asking why so many of our decisions are made behind a locked door, and handed down only when someone decides the waiting is complete. The answer is older than the Fed, and it is not about secrecy. It is about how a decision becomes a verdict.
